title: As the crow flies
concept: math · roots, rounding and nearly-equal numbers
description: Measure how far the treasure is in a straight line, and round the answers honestly.

tasks.title: Rounding, roots, and numbers that are nearly equal
tasks.body: math.sqrt() finds a square root, and math.hypot(a, b) the long side of a right-angled triangle. math.floor() rounds down, math.ceil() rounds up, and round(x, 2) rounds to 2 decimal places.
tasks.detail: Decimal numbers are stored in binary, so 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004, not 0.3. Compare such numbers with math.isclose(a, b), or round them before printing. round() rounds a number that is exactly half way to the nearest even number, so round(2.5) is 2.

tasks.code:
import math
print(0.1 + 0.2)
print(math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))
print(math.floor(-2.5), math.ceil(-2.5))
print(round(2.5), round(3.5))
print(math.hypot(3, 4))
tasks.note: 0.1 + 0.2 is very slightly more than 0.3, and isclose() allows for that. floor() and ceil() go down and up even for negative numbers, and round() picks the even neighbour for a half.

tasks.question: What does print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3) show?
tasks.why: == compares exactly, and 0.1 + 0.2 is stored as 0.30000000000000004. isclose() is the honest test for decimals.

tasks.prompt: Predict, then run: try round(0.5) and round(1.5). Then print math.sqrt(2), and round it to 3 places.

The treasure lies on the map grid. Ask how many squares east it is, then how many north, as whole numbers (either can be 0). Print three lines:

1. The straight-line distance to it, rounded to 2 decimal places.
2. How many squares the hero walks if they can only move along the grid, east plus north.
3. The straight-line distance rounded up to a whole number.
tasks.starter: # Import math, then measure the way to the treasure
hints: The straight-line distance is the square root of east squared plus north squared, or math.hypot(east, north) in one step.
round(x, 2) keeps two decimal places, and math.ceil() rounds up. The grid walk needs no square roots at all.
With other names: import math, then side = math.sqrt(area) and boxes = math.ceil(items / 6).

error_hints.text: math is a name only after import math at the top of the program.
Turn the replies into numbers with int(...) before working with them.
With 3 east and 4 north: 5.0 in a straight line, 7 along the grid, and 5 rounded up.
With 1 east and 1 north the distance is the square root of 2, so the first line is 1.41 and the last is 2.
Straight north, the distance is just the number north, as a decimal: 6.0.
Check a longer walk: round to 2 places, and round up for the last line, even when the decimal part is small.
Check a treasure at the start: everything is 0.

similar_example.code:
import math
area = 50
side = math.sqrt(area)
print(round(side, 1))
print(math.ceil(side))
similar_example.note: A square plot of 50: its side is a square root, rounded two ways. Your treasure needs the root of two squares added together.

other_ways.code:
import math
east = int(input("East? "))
north = int(input("North? "))
distance = math.hypot(east, north)
print(round(distance, 2))
print(east + north)
print(math.ceil(distance))
other_ways.note: hypot() works out the straight-line distance in one step.

other_ways.code:
from math import ceil
east = int(input("East? "))
north = int(input("North? "))
distance = (east ** 2 + north ** 2) ** 0.5
print(round(distance, 2))
print(east + north)
print(ceil(distance))
other_ways.note: ** 0.5 is a square root too. Only ceil() is needed from math.
